comment.value:
This paper conducts a review and analysis of citation screen datasets for systematic review automation. The authors consolidate and release a meta-dataset resource that includes collections from 9 previous resources, called LivSB, and conduct baseline experiments on screening classification using this dataset. 

Pros:
- Introduces a benchmark for SLR paper screening by collecting data from 9 resources, unifying their formats, and augmenting the dataset with additional data/metadata
- Provides baseline performance of several reasonable classification models
- Provides an analysis of past SLR screening datasets

Cons:
- Misalignment between title and content: One high level recommendation from the AC is to alter the title to more closely describe the scope of the work in the paper. This manuscript does not investigate or propose standarized evaluation for SLR automation; rather, it introduces a benchmark dataset for SLR publication screening. The title misconstrues the paper content and sets unrealistic expectations. I strongly recommend the title be changed.
- There are several other recommendations made by reviewers that must be incorporated in a revision, most notably addressing any data statistics inconsistencies, reporting results on the entire benchmark, reporting statistical significance, and fixing issues with the Streamlit app (dataset statistics are still broken). 

**I have some reservations about this manuscript, and would recommend conditional acceptance based on addressing the above issues if that were an option. However, since that's not an option, I am recommending acceptance and I am optimistic that the authors will address issues as necessary.**
Thank you for responses and updates. I have accordingly raised my score.

Thank you for your valuable feedback on our paper. We appreciate your thoughtful comments and suggestions for improvement. Below, we address each of your concerns and provide clarifications on the points you raised. Major changes in the manuscript are highlighted in red.

### 1. Detailed evaluation on each domain: 
We understand your interest in a more detailed evaluation of classification methods on individual domains, such as medical or computer science SLRs. Unfortunately, the domains we provided in Table 1 are only approximate and come from the original dataset creators (i.e., the difference between “clinical” and “drug” SLRs can be fuzzy and not clear). Moreover, for two datasets there are no clear categories, or reviews in these datasets are of a mixed type.

We were also considering distinguishing between types of systematic reviews (for instance, Cochrane differentiates reviews of Intervention/DTA/Qualitative/Prognosis). Unfortunately, out of ~300 SLRs, almost all available reviews fall only into the two DTA and Intervention reviews categories. In contrast, the other types have less than three reviews.

### 2. Data leakage problem: 
We apologise for the confusion about the data leakage problem. We discussed the data leakage problem in previous datasets in Section 3.3. Specifically, we found existing datasets with overlap and sometimes with substantial data leakage. Some SLRs are present in both training and test sets of the previous datasets, and some SLRs are common throughout collections. We curated datasets in the LivSB and ensured no contamination of the dataset. We have added a passage to Section 6 that this problem is sorted in LivSB by deduplicating the dataset.

Moreover, to ensure no contamination of the new LivSB-FT dataset, we opted for a time-wise split construction when designing the new full-text screening dataset so no old documents are included in the test set.

### 3. Clarification of Figure 1: 
We appreciate your feedback on Figure 1. We updated the example abstracts with English text in the revised version. Furthermore, we simplified the figure and removed the confusing mentions of "25th and 75th percentile word count". We also redesigned the Figure to match it with the flow of the newly added Section 2, “Task formulation”.

### 4. Speed of the screening algorithms: 
Thank you for your inquiry about the speed of the screening algorithms. In our study, we focused mainly on the performance of the algorithms in terms of accuracy. However, we understand the importance of speed, especially for large-scale SLRs. We included a discussion of the computational time of training and inference for Transformers models in the supplementary material (Appendix F.1).

### 5. Dataset accessibility issues: 
We recognise the challenges when switching from using publication titles and abstracts to full texts, particularly concerning dataset accessibility. We have decided to use only open-access publications, which limits the number of available documents to 25-35% of total publications in SLRs. However, it ensures the reproducibility of our dataset as all researchers will always have access to the same documents. Furthermore, by 2025 all systematic literature reviews published by Cochrane will be open-access [1] meaning that the ratio of available documents should only increase with time. We discuss the dataset accessibility issues, including potential licensing restrictions, in the revised manuscript.

---------

Once again, thank you for your insightful comments and suggestions. We believe that your feedback will significantly improve the quality of our paper. We look forward to your further feedback on our revised manuscript.

[1] https://www.cochrane.org/about-us/our-open-access-strategy

Thank you for your thorough review of our paper and for highlighting both the strengths and opportunities for improvement. We appreciate your feedback, and we have made the necessary changes to address your concerns (major changes in the manuscript are highlighted in red). Below are our responses to your suggestions:

### 1. Inconsistency in the number of reviews: 
We apologise for the lack of clarity and the inconsistency in the reported number of reviews across different sections of the paper. This difference is primarily due to three factors: (1) the difference in the number of reviews reported by one of the papers (in Table 1, we used the lower number -- now changed to the higher value), (2) in Table 1, we counted all SLRs from original datasets and didn’t account for the duplicated reviews, and (3) we weren't able to enhance all SLRs from original datasets so now the value in Table 2 is lower. The total number of SLRs from the original datasets is equal to 360. Our expanded, deduplicated dataset contains 322 unique SLRs. We have updated the numbers and the text in the paper, so it is more clear now.

### 2. Streamlit app and visualisations: 
We apologise for the issues with the streamlit app. We have fixed the broken app link and included relevant screenshots/figures in the paper. The streamlit app is now working properly under the following link [1].

### 3. Dataset Maintenance Plan: 
We understand the importance of maintaining the dataset for long-term use, especially given the reliance on external APIs for data loading. We plan to host the LivSB-FT full-text screening dataset at the TU Wien research repository (https://repositum.tuwien.at). Furthermore, recently Cochrane announced that by 2025 all systematic literature reviews published by them will be published as open-access, which should ensure data availability [2]. Hence, we are investigating the possibility of hosting and sharing the whole LivSB dataset directly.

### 4. Clarity of dataset sections: 
We have revised the dataset sections (previously Section 3, now Sections 4 and 5) to improve the flow and clarity of the paper. Section 4 now focuses solely on the description of the LivSB meta-dataset construction and its extension. Section 5 focuses only on the construction and experiments on the full-text screening dataset LivSB-FT.

### 5. Undefined Acronyms: 
We have updated the paper to include definitions for all acronyms at their first occurrence to avoid confusion.

### 6. Long-term Usefulness: 
We acknowledge the concerns regarding the reliance on machines for citation screening and the potential impact on research quality. Our benchmark provides the means for evaluating citation screening tools and hopefully will contribute to providing better quality algorithms. Nevertheless, in the limitations, we emphasise that human oversight is crucial in systematic literature reviews to ensure the selection of high-quality research.

### 7. Results on the entire benchmark:
We appreciate the reviewer's suggestion to include baseline results for the entire benchmark. Due to space constraints, we initially focused on reporting results only for the full-text screening dataset in the main paper. However, we recognise the importance of providing a comprehensive comparison and are actively working to incorporate the baseline results for the entire benchmark into the supplemental materials.

------

We hope that these revisions address your concerns and further improve the quality of our paper. Once again, we sincerely appreciate your insightful feedback and support in enhancing the work presented in our paper.

[1] https://systematic-review-datasets.streamlit.app/ 

[2] https://www.cochrane.org/about-us/our-open-access-strategy

Thank you for your insightful comments and suggestions. We appreciate your thorough review of our paper. Below, we address the concerns you raised and indicate how we have updated the manuscript in response (major changes in the manuscript are highlighted in red).

### 1. Lack of clear task formulation: 
Thank you for this suggestion. We fully agree that it will be important to provide a formal task definition. We have added a new "Task formulation" section in which we describe the input and output structures for our proposed model. We provide justifications for our task formulation, and present examples of inputs and outputs.

### 2. Clarity of the manuscript: 
We recognise that our manuscript may have been hard to follow due to the way details of pre-processing were mingled with the description of the introduced dataset. In response, we have revised the subsection "Dataset analysis" and moved it into the related work section (Section 3.3 Limitations of existing datasets in updated manuscript) to focus on the analysis and limitations of prior datasets, separating it from the introduction of the new datasets (Sections 4 and 5 in updated manuscript) to a separate section. We hope that this improves the clarity of the manuscript. 

### 3. Inconsistent and specialised vocabulary: 
We acknowledge the use of jargon and specialised vocabulary that might be unfamiliar to the broader NLP/IR audience. We have now provided explanations of the used terminology, including concepts such as "Cochrane", "review protocol", "review search strategy," and "review eligibility criteria." In Section 2, Task formulation, we also describe the meaning of terms such as "full-text screening" and "citation screening".

### 4. Clarifications on the meaning of "avg size" and "#docs": 
We apologise for the confusion regarding the terms "avg size" and "#docs" in Tables 1, 2, and 3. We have added an explanation to the tables to make it clear that "avg size" refers to the average document count in datasets (Table 1), and "#docs" refers to the total number of documents included in the dataset (Tables 2 and 3). Please note that the full-text screening dataset encompasses documents with uneven distribution across reviews, arising from variations in the availability of included/excluded publications for certain reviews. Consequently, we do not classify this dataset as a collection of Systematic Literature Reviews (SLRs), but rather treat it as a collection of independent documents.

### 5. Results in Table 4: 
We appreciate your suggestion to conduct significance tests and provide a discussion on the limitation of statistical significance. To mitigate this, we have evaluated the GPT-3.5-16k model on the full test dataset. Furthermore, we have conducted significance tests using McNemar’s t-test and found that only the Clinical-BigBird model on the LivSB-FT-TEST split showed statistically significant improvements compared to the stratified random baseline, Longformer, Clinical-Longformer, and GPT-3.5-turbo-16k models. We have added these updated results to the manuscript. The numbers in Table 4 are averaged over documents, not reviews.

### 6. Broken streamlit app: 
Thank you for bringing this to our attention. We have addressed the issue, and the streamlit app is now working properly under the following URL: https://systematic-review-datasets.streamlit.app/ 

------

Once again, we thank you for your thoughtful feedback. We hope that these revisions improve the clarity of our manuscript and make it more accessible to a broader audience. We believe that the changes we have made align with your recommendations and address your concerns.

Thank you for the detailed review and thoughtful feedback on our paper. We appreciate the time you took to assess our manuscript. We would like to respond to your concerns and offer explanations for our choices in the manuscript.

### 1. Contribution: 
We understand your concern regarding the novelty and significance of our contribution. While the primary contribution of our work is the unification of existing datasets, we believe that the value of our work goes beyond mere consolidation. By re-examining existing datasets and identifying common issues, we provide the community with a comprehensive, higher-quality, and easily accessible resource that can be instrumental in advancing the research in automated literature screening. We firmly believe that providing a unification of existing datasets is a crucial and necessary step towards the creation of a standardised evaluation benchmark, facilitating reproducibility and FAIRness. 

In addition to providing a unified dataset, we have introduced a new dataset LivSB-FT, specifically for evaluating full-text screening, which has not been previously considered in the literature. We have conducted experiments that provide a performance benchmark on this dataset, enabling new methods to conduct evaluations using a more robust evaluation framework. 

Finally, we would like to point out that our work follows a growing trend in the research community of contributing comprehensive benchmarks and meta-datasets aimed at consolidating and advancing the field. Notably, two papers also published at NeurIPS have laid similar groundwork in other domains: Thakur et al. in 2021 introduced "BEIR", a heterogeneous benchmark for zero-shot evaluation of information retrieval models [1], and Fries et al. in 2022 presented "BigBio", a framework for data-centric biomedical natural language processing [2].

### 2. Writing and Clarity: 
We acknowledge your concerns regarding the overall writing and clarity of the paper. We have revised the manuscript to provide a clearer problem formulation. We now include formal task definitions in Section 2. We also reduced the density of the writing, making the manuscript more accessible and easier to read. We have also separated previous datasets analysis from the LivSB dataset introduction section.

### 3. Experiment Section: 
We agree that the experiment section can benefit from a more in-depth analysis. In our revised version, we delved deeper into the experimental findings: for instance, we added the evaluation of the GPT3.5-16k model on the whole LivSB-FT-test dataset, we conducted the significance tests of the results, and we added the discussion on the speed of the screening algorithms.

------

We are grateful for acknowledging the strengths of our paper, particularly the contribution of a unified format for existing datasets. We believe that our work provides significant benefits to the research community in lowering the entry barrier for future research in the field of automated literature screening, contributing to the advancement of the field. Additionally, we understand that the identification of issues in previous benchmarks is valuable for the dataset and benchmark track of NeurIPS.

Thank you once again for your valuable insights.  We hope that we have addressed your comments in our revisions and are at your disposal to conduct any clarifications.


------


[1] Thakur, Nandan, Nils Reimers, Andreas Rücklé, Abhishek Srivastava, and Iryna Gurevych. _"BEIR: A heterogenous benchmark for zero-shot evaluation of information retrieval models."_ Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 2021, 35, 25792-25806.

[2] Fries, J., Weber, L., Seelam, N., Altay, G., Datta, D., Garda, S., ... & Beilharz, B. (2022). _"BigBio: a framework for data-centric biomedical natural language processing."_ Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 2022, 35, 25792-25806.

summary_and_contributions.value: The paper introduces a benchmark dataset for systematic literature reviews (SLR) - the authors aggregated existing datasets for SLR, created a consistent experimental setup for the aggregated datasets, and created supporting software tools to access the datasets via a unified API. Then the paper reports on some baseline experiments for SLR, treating the task as a long document text-pair classification task.

strengths.value:
- SLR is an important and impactful problem, creating resources for methodological communities to benchmark on this task is a meaningful contribution.
- The papers analysis of numerous past SLR datasets and the inconsistencies of their experimental setup is a useful analysis.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
- The paper does not seem to clearly state the proposed tasks at any point in the paper. I would strongly encourage discussion of what the input and output for a model would, ideally in a separate "task formulation" subsection with justifications for why a specific task formulation makes sense for the target application and perhaps a figure of example inputs and outputs. While the experiments seem to perform a text pair classification the appendix lists numerous other tasks for the dataset (eg question answering). 
- The paper is quite hard to follow. (elaborated below)

clarity.value:
- The paper is a little hard to follow because it melds a lot of the detail of pre-processing with the result of the pre-processing. For example, Sec 3.2, titled "dataset analysis" seems to discuss the limitations of prior datasets alongside a description of the introduced dataset, please consider moving this to a separate section of its own. 
- Further, the paper is likely not going to be consumable by the typical NLP/IR audience given that it uses a lot of inconsistent and specialized vocabulary - for example, are "full-text screening" and "citation screening" the same as an SLR task? As another example, "Every Cochrane SLR first registers and publishes the protocol containing the review scope, search strategy and the eligibility criteria" - consider describing "Cochrane," "protocol," "review-scope," "search strategy," and "eligibility criteria."
- Also related to the lack of clarity on the precise task, what do avg size and #docs in Table 1, Table 2, and Table 3 mean?
- I would encourage expanding Sec 2.2 also to introduce the norms and vocabulary of SLR. A task description section where you introduce with sufficient notation the predictive task being pursued. And a limitations/gaps section that describes the problem with prior datasets. And then move on to describing the aggregated dataset introduced here with consistent terminology.

additional_feedback.value:
- Are the numbers reported in Table 4 averaged over reviews or text-pairs? I would not expect the results to be statistically significant with 16 reviews in LIVSB-FT-TEST-SMALL. I understand that the cost of running LLM experiments is high, but i would encourage addition of significance tests and discussion of this limitation.
- The streamlit app linked in the appendix seems to be broken.

summary_and_contributions.value: This paper presents a benchmark for screening citations used in systematic literature reviews.  It performs a survey of 12 available systematic review datasets and includes 9 that are publicly available.  For all systematic reviews registered on Cochrane, it augments the existing datasets with substantial additional meta-data on article eligibility criteria, search strategy, and full-text of included articles (when available).   It compares a number of transformer models on the citation screening benchmark, finding GPT-4 to have the highest performance despite being tested zero-shot.

strengths.value:
* This paper provides a helpful & needed resource for systematic reviews of literature by enabling the comprehensive benchmarking of models used to screen citations for inclusion.  Not only does it unify the formatting of multiple datasets, but it also augments them with meaningful metadata from Cochrane to more closely match the data available for citation screening with protocols used in real life.  Doing so more closely matches the described task with clinical practice, improving the meaningfulness of benchmark results.
* The baseline examined for this benchmark provide a sufficiently diverse test of different methods that would reasonably be used for citation screening for systematic reviews.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
* The authors do not report the results of any model on the entire benchmark.  They only report results on the full-text screening subset constructed in the paper.   If you are releasing a benchmark, it is important to provide results on the entire benchmark rather than just a portion.
* The number of reviews included in this dataset is inconsistent.  For example, Table 1 lists 277 included reviews, Table 2 lists 322, and the abstract lists 280 -- which is it?
* The streamlit app to view the datasets/visualizations is broken.  It would be better if you included relevant screenshots/figures in the paper.

limitations.value:
The authors of this paper do address some of the limitations of how data must be downloaded due to copyright restrictions of the data providers, which may lead the dataset to break in the future without maintenance.  

One possible negative impact of this paper is the reliance on machines to perform the work of citation screening for systematic reviews, which may have negative impacts on the quality of the research presented in such reviews.

correctness.value:
* There are disagreements about the number of systematic reviews included in the benchmark.  For example, the abstract, table 1, and table 2 all list different numbers of systematic reviews in LIVSB
* The construction of the new dataset, LivSB-FT seems sound -- it gathers data on inclusion criteria and reasons for exclusion from Cochrane, which is the go-to source of truth for systematic literature reviews in the healthcare domain.  Moreover, it

clarity.value:
While this paper makes significant contributions and is reasonably well written overall, a few edits would improve the clarity:
* Section 3 on the LivSB dataset is very long and meanders between multiple topics.  It begins with the creation of the core benchmark from its constituent datasets, then performs an analysis of the original dataset before returning back to other aspects of dataset construction.  Similarly, section 3.4 alternates between talking about the addition of the full-text of screened articles and how this could potentially be modeled as a natural language inference task.  Section 3 would be much clearer overall if it focused on only describing the dataset construction.  Aspects of analysis/modeling should be placed after the description of the dataset rather than mixed in.
* Multiple acronyms are used which are never defined (e.g. DTA, NLI, etc)
* Additional documentation of the data would be helpful -- e.g what are the data fields, how is the data formatted upon download, etc.  The data is said to use the BigBio Schema -- which schema category does it fall under?

relation_to_prior_work.value: It is clear that this work differs from prior work by aggregating multiple citation screening datasets into a single benchmark, as well as adding a full-text citation screening task.

documentation.value:
* A URL for review access is provided and lists a license for the data
* A data card providing many details of the dataset is in the supplement (although more details on the available data fields would be even better).
* I cannot seem to find a data maintenance plan.  Such a plan is very important for the long-term usefulness of this dataset since it must be loaded from external APIs due to copyright considerations and there is the possibility that these could change.

ethics.value: This paper takes care to not include datasets that are not publicly available.  No other ethics concerns are present.

summary_and_contributions.value: Kusa et al. did a benchmark on systematic literature review process. To do that, they concatenated several existing SLR datasets and curated a dataset that is based on the full text. Then they benchmarked performances of several classification methods on citation screening. The resource and the practice of screening full text for citation screening would be useful to the scientific community.

strengths.value:
Provided a meta-collection of SLR dataset and curated SLRs for full text screening.

Benchmarked methods for full text screening.

Such resources would be useful to the research community though the current performance is not very satisfying.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
The authors benchmarked the classification methods on the combined meta-dataset, it would be interesting to see a more detailed evaluation on each domain (e.g. clinical, comp. science).

Data leakage problem seems to be a big issue in such evaluation, but I didn't find if and how the data leakage problem is resolved in this paper.

clarity.value: Figure 1 was not clear to me: the example abstracts are not in English, and I don't get what 25th and 75th percentile word count mean in the figure legend. It would help the general audience by laying out the output format and incorporating the screening methods used to this workflow.

flag_for_ethics_review.value: 2: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

additional_feedback.value:
How fast are the screening algorithms?

Are there dataset accessibility issue when switching from using abstract to full text?

title.value: CSMeD: Bridging the Dataset Gap in Automated Citation Screening for Systematic Literature Reviews

abstract.value: Systematic literature reviews (SLRs) play an essential role in summarising, synthesising and validating scientific evidence. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in using machine learning techniques to automate the identification of relevant studies for SLRs. However, the lack of standardised evaluation datasets makes comparing the performance of such automated literature screening systems difficult. In this paper, we analyse the citation screening evaluation datasets, revealing that many of the available datasets are either too small, suffer from data leakage or have limited applicability to systems treating automated literature screening as a classification task, as opposed to, for example, a retrieval or question-answering task. To address these challenges, we introduce CSMED, a meta-dataset consolidating nine publicly released collections, providing unified access to 325 SLRs from the fields of medicine and computer science. CSMED serves as a comprehensive resource for training and evaluating the performance of automated citation screening models. Additionally, we introduce CSMED-FT, a new dataset designed explicitly for evaluating the full text publication screening task. To demonstrate the utility of CSMED, we conduct experiments and establish baselines on new datasets.

TLDR.value: CSMeD is a consolidated meta-dataset addressing the limitations of existing datasets in evaluating automated citation screening for systematic literature reviews, offering unified access to 325 SLRs and introducing a new full text screening dataset.

dateprocesses.script:
def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
